summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, following a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights programme. The Human Dignity Trust records the case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-sodomy statutes across nearby island jurisdictions. A High Court ruling on sodomy, published May 2023, held discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional. Under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, 'serious indecency' carried a maximum of ten years' imprisonment where committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older.

Regional litigation was also live. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging Sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act; the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019, and failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent. In February 2018 Brandon Coward attacked Hoffmann with a meat cleaver, causing serious injuries including to her throat. He was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Employment is the sharpest documented exposure for trans people. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status. Hoffmann argues the Act excludes trans workers, because 'gender identity' and 'gender expression' are not listed as protected grounds; reporting from August 2020 describes trans Barbadians as frequently fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'. No identity-document process or legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians is covered by the available sources.

No same-sex relationship or union is recognised. The government ruled out same-sex marriage in June 2016 and in September 2020 announced only a plan to recognise 'some form' of civil union, followed by a referendum on gay marriage; critics called the proposal 'unnecessarily vague' and expected the referendum to fail, and neither had been enacted as of the source's account. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal though not explicitly prohibited or regulated, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The Barbados Fertility Centre offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

Entry and screening carry documented hostility. Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category, and the government has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration: in 2011 it said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean said such applications risked abusing the Canadian refugee system, noting two of nine Canadian applications had been denied. A 2016 Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the UK and the US, and UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations. In July 2020 the government's 'Welcome Stamp' remote-work visa initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse; the rule was changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Official and religious hostility remains prominent. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite stated Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage and, after UK Prime Minister David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM aid warning over sodomy laws, said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a 'cheap political trick' as its report did not mention same-sex marriage. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and American evangelical ministers have, according to human rights activists, spread anti-gay rhetoric more widely. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected May 2018, is reported as pro-LGBT.

Trans people are visible and organising under threat. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in Barbados in November 2018, with a local ally organisation, veteran trans advocates and Hoffmann's first-person account of visibility and danger on the island. Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue; Pride events have run since a small gathering in November 2017 and a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018.
tangentialFactors:
Barbados sits within a regional pattern of colonial-era anti-sodomy statutes being struck down through constitutional litigation rather than legislation, and its December 2022 decriminalisation belongs to that pattern rather than to an isolated domestic reform.

The 2018 Inter-American Commission petition means the statutory framework could still change through a binding regional court decision, independent of Barbadian parliamentary action.

Public hostility is organised rather than incidental: fundamentalist churches, arriving foreign evangelical ministers, and an informal newspaper comment line opposing a proposed gay tourism package have all been recorded, while the Anglican and Catholic churches hold a different position on the former buggery law.

Post-colonial sovereignty rhetoric shapes official responses. The 2011 Commonwealth summit aid warning from the United Kingdom produced a public refusal to be dictated to, and a subsequent ministerial claim about externally imposed same-sex marriage drew a rebuke from Human Rights Watch.
localsOnly:
Trans Barbadians face documented employment loss: the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020 does not list gender identity or gender expression as protected grounds, and trans workers are described as frequently fired or refused work for their presentation.

No legal gender recognition or identity-document process for trans people is established in the sources, so residents appear to have no route to align official documents with their gender.

Residents have no recognised relationship status with a same-sex partner. The September 2020 announcement of a civil union with a follow-on referendum on same-sex marriage had not been enacted, leaving couples without inheritance, hospital-visit or next-of-kin standing.

Family formation is constrained by adoption law, the illegal status of surrogacy and the absence of same-sex couples being recognised as families. Community organisations including BGLAD and a Trans Day of Remembrance vigil have operated since 2013 and 2018 respectively, giving residents some organised support.
